title: Ruling 2022-06: Vermont Resident Working in New Hampshire Has Not Abandoned Vermont Domicile
text:
Date: November 2, 2022

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client, [Taxpayer] (Taxpayer), regarding the applicability of Vermont income tax to her 2022 taxable income. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [date].

Facts 

1. Taxpayer recently moved from Vermont to New Hampshire for a job that started on [date].

2. Taxpayer has rented a 2-bedroom, 2-bathroom apartment in [City], New Hampshire.

3. Taxpayer and her husband own a 3-bedroom, 2-bathroom home in [City], Vermont. Her husband plans to stay at the [City] house when he is in Vermont during the work week.

4. Taxpayer will spend most of her time in New Hampshire, including the entire work week as well as many weekends. She may travel to Vermont on some weekends and may travel to Vermont to visit family and friends or for vacations.

5. Most of Taxpayer’s personal possessions are in New Hampshire, including certain things that are near and dear to her like her jewelry, camera, video camera, and most of her photographs.

6. Taxpayer’s only job will be as an [position] at [workplace] in [City], New Hampshire. She will work in person at the office, as well as [numerous locations] in New Hampshire.

7. Taxpayer’s husband will be in New Hampshire 2 to 3 work days a week and on many weekends. He is employed by a Vermont-based company and will work in-person in Vermont approximately two to three days a week and work remotely from New Hampshire on the other

work days.

8. Taxpayer’s parents and siblings reside in Vermont and she has no children.

9. Taxpayer has registered her car in New Hampshire and plans to obtain a New Hampshire driver’s license by [date].

10. Taxpayer plans to register to vote in New Hampshire.

Discussion 

Vermont law of domicile 

Vermont income tax is imposed on all the income of every resident, and on income of every nonresident from sources within the State. 32 V.S.A. § 5822(a), (b). “Residency” is defined as follows:

(11) “Residency.”

(A) An individual qualifies for residency in this State for that portion of the taxable year during which:

(i) the individual is domiciled in this State; or

(ii) the individual maintains a permanent place of abode within this State if the individual both maintains a permanent place of abode and is present in this State for more than an aggregate of 183 days of that taxable year.

32 V.S.A. § 5811(11).

“Domicile” is defined in the Department’s income tax regulations:

Section 2 Definition of Domicile

(a) Domicile means the place where an individual has a true, fixed permanent home, and to which place, whenever the person is absent, he or she has the intention of returning. An individual may have several places of abode in a year, but at no time can he or she have more than one domicile. Domicile is not limited to a specific structure, but refers rather to a place or an area to which the individual expects to return. Department of Taxes Regulations (Eff. 8/06/04) (“Regs.”) §§ 1.5811(11)(A)(1), Sec. 2(a).

A husband and wife are presumed to have the same domicile:

It is presumed that the domiciles of a husband and wife . . . are the same, unless there is affirmative evidence to the contrary. However, spouses who are separated may acquire separate domiciles, even though no judgment or decree of separation has been rendered provided the requisite move and intent are present. Id. at Sec. 6.

Once established, a domicile is never lost unless there is both (1) a change to a new place of residence and (2) abandonment of the former residence. Id. at Sec. (2)(c).

Taxpayer bears the burden of proving a change of domicile by clear and convincing evidence. Id. at Sec. 5(a), (b). Intent to change domicile must be “manifested by unequivocal acts.” Id. at Sec. 5(b).

“The fact that a change of domicile was motivated primarily by a desire to gain a tax advantage is immaterial if the intention of the individual to acquire a new domicile is absolute and fixed and the actions of the individual confirm that intention.” Id. at Sec. 4(a).

“An individual who is in transit between old and new domiciles is domiciled in the old domicile until the new one is established.” Id. at Sec. 2(e).

The regulations describe factors to consider in determining a domicile:

Section 3 Relevant Factors

The factors which are deemed of primary relevance to a fair determination of an individual’s domicile are the facts and circumstances that are not readily changeable by the taxpayer in order to alter their domicile for tax reasons. The following factors, in no particular order, shall be considered in determining an individual’s domicile.

(a) Home. The Department will consider what residences are owned or rented (for the taxpayer’s use) by the taxpayer; where they are located; how they are used; and the sizes, values and uses of each residence.

(b) Time. The Department will consider where and how the individual spends time during the tax year; whether the taxpayer is retired or actively involved in a business or profession; how much the individual travels; the nature of the travel; where the individual spends time when not required to be at a location for employment reasons, and the overall pattern of residence of the individual.

(c) Items Near and Dear. The Department will consider where items or possessions that the individual considers “near and dear” to his or her heart are located, e.g. items of significant sentimental value, family heirlooms, collections of valuables or possessions that enhance the quality of the individual’s life.

(d) Active Business Involvement. The Department will consider how the individual earns a living; where the individual's place of employment is; whether the individual is actively involved in any business ownership or professions, and if so, the degree; where the business or professional office is located and the ;proportion of in-state to out-of-state business activities. “Actively involved” means the individual participates in the day-to-day operation, or in a policymaking position, of a business.

(e) Family Connections. The Department will consider where members of the individual’s immediate family reside; where minor children attend school, and the type of school facility. “Immediate family” means the spouse, civil union partner, child, or parent of an individual.

Other factors which may be considered include home address and legal residence listed on federal tax returns, place where the individual is registered to vote, place of vehicle registration, state of driver’s or professional license, place of club and organization memberships, place where mail is received. There may be other similar factors. However, because these factors may be altered without a true commitment to such location they will generally not carry as much weight as factors (a) through (e) above.

Id. at Sec. 3. In addition to these factors, several others are considered, particularly with regard

to a claimed change of domicile:

1. location of domicile for prior years;

2. registration as voter;

3. voting by absentee ballot;

4. place of filing of federal income tax returns;

5. filing and payment of state income taxes;

6. declaration of place of residence in will;

7. recitals in deeds and legal documents;

8. written and oral declarations generally;

9. situs of bank accounts and securities;

10. membership in churches, clubs, lodges, societies;

11. automobile registration and license;

12. claiming or filing homestead exemptions;

13. school attended by minor children.

Id. at Sec. 4(b). None of these factors are conclusive; they are weighed in view of all the facts. Id.

Application of the law to Taxpayer’s facts 

At least until [month] of this year, Taxpayer’s domicile was Vermont, her true, fixed permanent home where she owns a house and resides with her husband. Her Vermont domicile will not be lost unless she successfully changes her place of residence and takes unequivocal steps to abandon her Vermont domicile. Taxpayer must prove her change of domicile by clear and convincing evidence. See Quazzo v. Dep't of Taxes, 2014 VT 81 (2014).

The evidence presented does not support a finding that Taxpayer has changed her domicile to New Hampshire:

Home. Taxpayer owns a 3-bedroom, 2-bathroom house with her husband in Vermont; she has rented a 2-bedroom, 2-bathroom apartment in New Hampshire. Taxpayer’s ownership of the Vermont house, and the fact that the house is larger than an apartment she rents in New

Hampshire, weigh in favor of Vermont domicile.

Time. Taxpayer will spend the entire work week in New Hampshire, and most weekends. This weighs in favor of New Hampshire domicile.

Items near and dear. Taxpayer’s jewelry, camera, video camera, and most of her photographs are in her New Hampshire apartment. There is no evidence of what items Taxpayer keeps at her Vermont house, or where she keeps her important papers, family heirlooms, items of historical or sentimental value, or other significant personal items. This evidence is too incomplete to weigh in favor of either location.

Active business involvement. Taxpayer’s place of business is in New Hampshire. This weighs in favor of New Hampshire domicile.

Family connections. Taxpayer’s husband, parents and siblings live in Vermont. There is no evidence of New Hampshire relatives. This weighs in favor of Vermont domicile.

Miscellaneous other factors. Taxpayer will register her vehicle in New Hampshire, obtain a New Hampshire driver’s license and register to vote in New Hampshire. These facts weigh in favor of New Hampshire domicile. The regulations, however, state that these factors may be altered without a true commitment to location, and do not carry as much weight as other factors. It is not known whether Taxpayer has changed her address on various credit card and other accounts or will continue to receive mail at her Vermont address - factors which could weigh in favor of Vermont domicile.

It is not known what address Taxpayer will use for her Federal income tax returns, where she declares her place of residence in her will, if any, what address she will use on her credit card and other accounts, whether she will retain Vermont bank accounts, whether she will continue to see Vermont doctors and dentists, and whether she and her husband will declare their [City] house as a homestead (domicile) for purposes of [City] property tax. These are all indicia of domicile.

Of the known factors, two weigh in favor of New Hampshire: time spent in New Hampshire and location of her employment; two weigh in favor of Vermont domicile: the Vermont house and husband’s residence in the Vermont house. The New Hampshire car registration and

driver’s license and New Hampshire voter registration weigh in favor of New Hampshire domicile, but do not carry as much weight as the other factors. Continuing ownership of the Vermont house and the fact that her husband continues to reside there, coupled with the fact that Taxpayer intends to return there periodically to visit her husband, family and friends, indicate steps to abandon her Vermont domicile.

Since the intent to change domicile must be manifested by unequivocal acts, and since proof of change of domicile must be clear and convincing, the evidence here is insufficient to prove a change of domicile or to project a change of domicile for future years. Taxpayer’s domicile remains Vermont. Her New Hampshire salary will be subject to Vermont personal income tax.

General Provisions 

Issuance of this ruling is conditioned upon the understanding that neither the taxpayer nor a related taxpayer is currently under audit or involved in an administrative appeal or litigation concerning the subject matters of the ruling. This ruling is issued solely to the taxpayer and is limited to the facts presented, as affected by current statutes and regulations.

Other taxpayers may refer to this ruling, when redacted to protect confidentiality, to see the Department's general approach, but the Department will not be bound by this ruling in the case of any other taxpayer or in the case of any change in the relevant statutes or regulations.

This ruling will be made public after deletion of the taxpayer’s name and any information which may identify the taxpayer. A copy of this ruling showing the proposed deletions is attached, and you may request within 30 days that the Commissioner delete any further information that might identify the taxpayer. The final discretion as to deletions rests with the Commissioner.

You have the right to appeal this ruling within 30 days. 3 V.S.A. §§ 808, 815.
